questions.prompt: Which of these formulas is in CNF (clause normal form, also called conjunctive normal form)?
questions.explain: CNF is a conjunction of clauses, and a clause is a disjunction of literals. `(P ∨ ¬Q) ∧ R` has the two clauses `P ∨ ¬Q` and `R`. The tempting wrong answer `(P ∧ ¬Q) ∨ R` is the other way round, an OR of ANDs, which is disjunctive normal form. The other two still contain a negation in front of a bracket or an arrow.

questions.prompt: Convert the formula to CNF. The result is one clause. Type it with the literals in alphabetical order, with `-` for ¬ and `v` for ∨, without spaces.
questions.explain: Remove the arrow first: `¬P ∨ ¬(Q ∧ R)`. Then De Morgan turns `¬(Q ∧ R)` into `¬Q ∨ ¬R`, so everything is one clause: `¬P ∨ ¬Q ∨ ¬R`. The trap is to keep the ∧ and write two clauses, or to forget one of the two negations. De Morgan flips the connective and negates both parts.

questions.prompt: One line of this CNF conversion is wrong. Which one, and why?
questions.code:
start    P → (Q ∧ (R ∨ S))
line 1   ¬P ∨ (Q ∧ (R ∨ S))
line 2   (¬P ∨ Q) ∧ (R ∨ S)
line 3   clauses: ¬P ∨ Q  and  R ∨ S
options: Line 2: `¬P` must go into both parts, so the second part is `¬P ∨ R ∨ S`
Line 2: `Q ∧ (R ∨ S)` must first become `(Q ∧ R) ∨ (Q ∧ S)`
Line 3: `R ∨ S` must be split into two unit clauses
questions.explain: Distribution puts the outside part into **both** inner parts: `A ∨ (B ∧ C)` becomes `(A ∨ B) ∧ (A ∨ C)`. So line 2 must be `(¬P ∨ Q) ∧ (¬P ∨ R ∨ S)`. Line 1 is fine, because `P → X` becomes `¬P ∨ X`. The traps: distributing ∧ over ∨ leads away from CNF, and a disjunction is one clause that is never split.

questions.prompt: The knowledge base `{ P ↔ Q, ¬(Q ∨ R) }` is converted to CNF. How many clauses does the clause set have?
questions.explain: `P ↔ Q` gives two clauses, one for each direction: `¬P ∨ Q` and `¬Q ∨ P`. `¬(Q ∨ R)` becomes `¬Q ∧ ¬R`, which is two unit clauses. Together that makes 4. The trap is to read `¬(Q ∨ R)` as the single clause `¬Q ∨ ¬R` and count 3.
